[out.audio](#outaudio), [out.audio_file](#outaudio_file), [out.dmx](#outdmx), [out.mesh](#outmesh), [out.ndi](#outndi), [out.projector](#outprojector), [out.spout](#outspout), [out.table](#outtable), [out.video](#outvideo)

### out.audio

Plays sound on a speaker or headphones, always through a limiter that keeps it below -1 dBFS

Follows the show clock: cooks again whenever time moves.

Inputs:

- `in` (audio): The sound to play: mono plays on every speaker, stereo on left and right

Outputs: none.

| param | type | default | range | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `device` | text |  |  | Part of the output's name (the menu beside it lists them), e.g. `Speakers`; empty: the system's default output. Several out.audio nodes on one device are added together |
| `active` | bool | `true` |  | Off: plays nothing, and the device closes when no other node uses it |
| `level` | float | `0` | -60 to 12 dB (soft) | The volume, in dB: 0 plays the sound as it comes, -6 at half the amplitude. A change glides across one frame. The limiter comes after it |
| `mute` | bool | `false` |  | Silence, faded across one frame; the device stays open. audio.mute mutes every output at once |
| `reverb` | float | `0.2` | 0 to 1 (soft) | How much room the sound gets: 0 plays it dry, 0.2 a small room you just notice, 1 only the room. A mono sound gets stereo width from it |
| `room` | float | `0.4` | 0 to 1 (soft) | The size of the room: how long the sound rings on. 0 dies away in 0.3 s, 0.4 in 0.85 s, 0.7 in 1.8 s, 1 in 4 s |
| `damping` *(more)* | float | `0.5` | 0 to 1 (soft) | How much faster high tones die away in the room: 0 as fast as low ones, 0.5 in about half the time, 1 in a tenth. More sounds warmer and duller |
| `latency` *(more)* | float | `50` | 20 to 200 (soft) | Milliseconds of sound queued ahead of the device, which adds its own buffer on top. Less answers faster; too little and late frames are heard as gaps (audio.status counts them as underruns) |

### out.audio_file

Records sound to a WAV file: its input, or everything the out.audio nodes play

Follows the show clock: cooks again whenever time moves.

Inputs:

- `in` (audio): The sound to record with `source` at input: any number of channels up to 64

Outputs: none.

| param | type | default | range | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `record` | bool | `false` |  | Recording while on: turning record on starts a new file, turning record off finishes the file. The record button above and audio_file_out.start / .stop switch this param; bind it to a channel to start and stop from OSC or a button. A project always opens with record off |
| `source` | input \| all | `"input"` |  | What is recorded, fixed when the recording starts; input: the sound wired to `in`, as it comes, with its rate and channels; all: what every out.audio of the project plays, added up as the speakers get it, in stereo (audio.mute silences the room, not the file). No out.audio: nothing is recorded |
| `format` | pcm24 \| float32 | `"pcm24"` |  | How the samples are stored, fixed when the recording starts; pcm24: 24-bit integers, what editing programs expect. Sound above full scale is clipped; float32: 32-bit floats, in files a third larger. Sound above full scale is kept, for an input without a limiter |
| `file` | text |  |  | The WAV file, relative to the project; empty records to recordings/<node name>.wav. A file that exists is never overwritten: the recording gets the next free name with _2, _3, ... |

### out.dmx

Sends channels to DMX lights and fixtures: Enttec Open DMX USB, Art-Net, sACN or DDP

Inputs:

- `chans` (chan)

Outputs: none.

| param | type | default | range | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `protocol` | open_dmx \| art_net \| sacn \| ddp | `"open_dmx"` |  | How the slots leave this machine; open_dmx: an Enttec Open DMX USB on a serial port, one universe; art_net: Art-Net over UDP, to a node or as a broadcast; sacn: sACN (E1.31) over UDP, to each universe's multicast group or a host; ddp: DDP over UDP to a pixel controller such as WLED, no universes |
| `port` | text |  |  | Serial port of the Open DMX USB, such as COM5 or /dev/ttyUSB0; empty takes the first FTDI FT232R plugged in (dmx.ports lists them) |
| `host` | text |  |  | IP address to send to, optionally with :port. Empty broadcasts Art-Net and sends sACN to the multicast groups. DDP needs an address |
| `universe` | int | `1` | 0 to 16 (soft) | Universe of the first slot, as the protocol counts (Art-Net from 0, sACN from 1); more than 512 slots spill into the next. Not used by the Open DMX USB and DDP |
| `address` | int | `1` | 1 to 512 (soft) | DMX address (slot, from 1) the first channel goes to; for DDP the byte, from 1 |
| `values` | unit \| byte | `"unit"` |  | What the channel values mean; unit: 0 to 1, sent as 0 to 255; byte: 0 to 255, sent as they are (rounded) |
| `rate` | float | `30` | 1 to 60 Hz (soft) | Frames per second, sent whether or not anything changed; the Open DMX USB manages about 35 |

### out.mesh

Writes its input geometry to an OBJ, STL or glb file

Inputs:

- `in` (geo): The geometry to write

Outputs: none.

| param | type | default | range | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `file` | file (obj, stl, glb) |  |  | The file to write, relative to the project; empty writes export/<node name>.obj (.stl, .glb with that format). The node creates the export folder but no other |
| `overwrite` | bool | `true` |  | On: every write replaces the file, for a program that keeps reading it. Off: every write makes a new file with the next free name (_2, _3, ...); in mode changes that is a new file per change |
| `format` | auto \| obj \| stl \| glb | `"auto"` |  | The file format. Each is written so geo.file with up auto reads it back upright; auto: by extension, obj for any other; obj: text, y up, one object per part, no materials; stl: binary, z up, one solid without parts or materials; glb: binary glTF, y up, one node per part, material colours |
| `mode` | changes \| manual | `"changes"` |  | When the node writes; changes: whenever the geometry differs from what was written; manual: only on the command mesh_out.write |
| `instances` | expand \| skip | `"expand"` |  | What happens to copies from geo.tex_instance. At most 4194304 triangles and 65536 parts are written; expand: one copy per texel, read back from the GPU, each its own part. For copies that move every frame use mode manual; skip: each model once, where it stands without its copies |

### out.ndi

Sends a picture, and sound if wired, over the network as an NDI® source, to other programs and computers; needs the NDI runtime (ndi.video)

Inputs:

- `in` (tex): The picture to send
- `audio` (audio): Sound to send with the picture: any rate from 8000 to 192000 samples per second, up to 16 channels. Pictures and sound then carry the show time, so receivers keep them in step

Outputs: none.

| param | type | default | range | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | text |  |  | The source name receivers pick. NDI puts the machine's name before the source name, as in `PC (name)`. Empty: `penumbra` and the node's name, such as `penumbra ndi1` |
| `alpha` | straight \| premultiplied \| opaque | `"opaque"` |  | How transparency travels to the receivers. With alpha, NDI sends an extra plane, which costs about twice the CPU and some latency; straight: colour and alpha apart, as most programs take it; premultiplied: colour multiplied by alpha; opaque: no transparency: sent over black, or a received alpha ignored |

### out.projector

Shows a picture fullscreen on a projector or display, or in a part of it, with colour correction to match projectors; or in a window on the desktop, as a preview

Follows the show clock: cooks again whenever time moves.

Inputs:

- `in` (tex)
- `gain` (tex)
- `black` (tex)

Outputs: none.

| param | type | default | range | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `display` | text |  |  | Display id from output.list, e.g. `EPSON PJ [SECA519] @ target 168194` (model and connector) or `AW3225QF [DELA246 #BY4BYZ3]` (model and serial number). The monitor name alone works when unique |
| `active` | bool | `true` |  | Open the output window on its display. Off closes the window and the node does nothing: its inputs are not cooked for it, so a chain only it shows costs nothing |
| `window` | bool | `false` |  | Show the picture in a window of its own on the desktop instead of fullscreen on `display`: a preview beside the editor, also on the editor's display. It keeps running smoothly while the editor is minimised. Move and resize it like any window; closing it turns `active` off. `display` and `viewport` do not apply |
| `borderless` | bool | `false` |  | With `window` on: the window without title bar and frame, only the picture. Drag the picture to move the window, drag its edge to resize it |
| `window_place` *(more)* | vec4 | `[0, 0, 0, 0]` | px | With `window` on: x, y, width and height of the window in desktop pixels, as output.list gives the displays. x and y are the window's top left corner, title bar included; width and height the picture's size. Moving or resizing the window writes it here, so the window opens there again. All 0: where Windows puts a new window, 960 x 540. A place off every connected display is not taken: the window opens as with all 0, and the place stays until the window is moved |
| `fit` | fit \| fill \| stretch | `"fit"` |  | How the picture sits in the viewport when their aspects differ; fit: all visible, black bars; fill: covered, cropped; stretch: covered, distorted |
| `viewport` *(more)* | vec4 | `[0, 0, 1, 1]` | 0 to 1 | x, y, width, height inside the display, in display sizes (a quarter of a 4K splitter: 0, 0, 0.5, 0.5) |
| `test` | bool | `false` |  | A test pattern in the projector's own pixels instead of the input, in this projector's colour (white when it is the only one showing a test pattern, else one that keeps overlapping projectors apart): see `test_pattern`. projector.test switches every projector at once |
| `test_pattern` | align \| focus \| motion \| fields | `"align"` |  | Which test pattern `test` shows; align: square cells, centre cross and circle, the image's edge: keystone, overscan, alignment; focus: one-pixel checkers and lines in patches at the corners and the centre, where defocus shows first, over a one-pixel grid; the patches sit lower for the second projector and lower again for the third, so stacked projectors show them side by side; motion: moves on by whole pixels each frame the output presents: two bars, a strip of 30 cells lit one after another, the frame count and how many frames penumbra presented late; stutter with 0 late comes from after the GPU (cable, extender, projector); fields: full white, red, green, blue and black, 3 seconds each, uncorrected, for dead and stuck pixels; projectors showing it take turns, the others black meanwhile |
| `correct` *(colour)* | bool | `true` |  | Apply the colour correction below. Off shows the plain picture, to compare. The test pattern is never corrected |
| `strength` *(colour)* | float | `1` | 0 to 1 | How much of the correction applies, matrix and curves alike: 1 all of it, 0 the projector uncorrected. A lower value keeps more of a brighter projector's brightness, but leaves more of the difference in colour and brightness between projectors |
| `gain` *(colour)* | float | `1` | 0 to 1 | Brightness by hand, in linear light, on top of the matrix (0.8: a fifth less light) |
| `matrix` *(colour)* | text |  |  | 3x3 matrix in linear light, drive = matrix x colour. Three rows of three numbers (`1 0 0 / 0 1 0 / 0 0 1`); empty is none. projector.match writes this matrix |
| `curves` *(colour)* | text |  |  | Tone curve per channel, from drive (sRGB-encoded, evenly spaced from 0 to 1) to the signal sent. Lines `r: 0 0.06 ... 1`, `g: ...`, `b: ...` with 2 to 64 samples each, or one line for all three. A straight line 0..1 or empty is none. projector.match writes these curves |
| `flatten` *(colour)* | float | `1` | 0 to 1 | How much of the gain map at the `gain` input applies: 1 all of it (even brightness and colour across the picture), 0 none. projector.flatfield measures the map |
| `lift` *(colour)* | float | `1` | 0 to 4 | Scales the black lift at the `black` input: 1 as measured, 0 none. Raise it where the camera underrated the black (black outside an overlap still darker than inside). projector.flatfield measures the lift |

### out.video

Records its input to a movie file (H.264 or ProRes)

Follows the show clock: cooks again whenever time moves.

Inputs:

- `in` (tex): The picture to record
- `audio` (audio): Sound for the file, with `audio` at auto or input: any rate, the first two channels (mono on both)

Outputs: none.

| param | type | default | range | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `record` | bool | `false` |  | Recording while on: turning record on starts a new file, turning record off finishes the file. The record button above and video_out.start / .stop switch this param; bind it to a channel to start and stop from OSC or a button. A project always opens with record off. While off, the picture's chain is not cooked for this node: a chain only it takes costs nothing |
| `codec` | h264 \| prores_422 \| prores_422_hq \| prores_4444 | `"h264"` |  | What the picture is encoded as (the file's extension follows it); h264: H.264 in MP4: small files any player opens; 4:2:0, 8 bits, high constant quality; prores_422: Apple ProRes 422 in MOV: for editing, every frame a keyframe; about 37 MB/s at 1080p60; prores_422_hq: Apple ProRes 422 HQ in MOV: as 422 at a higher rate, about 55 MB/s at 1080p60; prores_4444: Apple ProRes 4444 in MOV with alpha: 4:4:4, 12 bits, the transparency kept; the largest files |
| `audio` | auto \| input \| all \| off | `"auto"` |  | Where the file's sound comes from, fixed when the recording starts; auto: input while something is wired to the audio input, all while nothing is; input: the sound wired to the audio input, also when no out.audio plays it; AAC in an MP4, 24-bit PCM in a MOV. Nothing wired: no sound; all: what every out.audio of the project plays, added up as the speakers get it (audio.mute silences the room, not the file); AAC in an MP4, 24-bit PCM in a MOV. No out.audio: no sound; off: no sound |
| `preset` | fast \| balanced \| best | `"fast"` |  | How hard the H.264 encoder works per frame: faster drops fewer frames of a busy picture, slower keeps more fine detail; fast: the fastest: Baseline profile, constant quality 23; files no larger than balanced's, fine detail a little softer; 20 to 45 % faster than balanced on busy pictures; balanced: High profile, constant quality 18, the encoder's quickest search; best: High profile, quality 18, a wider search: slightly smaller files, a third slower than balanced; for calm pictures, smaller sizes or lower rates |
| `encoder` *(more)* | auto \| cpu \| gpu | `"auto"` |  | Where the H.264 is encoded: on the graphics card it keeps up with 1440p and 4K at 60 fps; auto: the graphics card's encoder when this machine has one (NVIDIA NVENC), else the CPU; the status says which and why; cpu: the CPU, with `threads` threads, as on every machine; gpu: the graphics card's encoder; without one the recording fails and says why |
| `file` | text |  |  | The movie file, relative to the project; empty records to recordings/<node name>. A file that exists is never overwritten: the recording gets the next free name with _2, _3, ... |
| `rate` | float | `0` (show rate) | 0 to 120 Hz (soft) | Frames per second of the file. Frames follow the show clock: a slower show makes frames last longer, a faster show leaves some out; 0: show rate |
| `size` | input \| fixed | `"input"` |  | The picture size of the file, fixed when the recording starts; input: the input's size when recording starts (rounded down to even); fixed: width x height; the input is scaled to it, aspect not kept |
| `width` | int | `1920` | 16 to 3840 (soft) | Width of the file in pixels with `size` fixed (rounded down to even) |
| `height` | int | `1080` | 16 to 2160 (soft) | Height of the file in pixels with `size` fixed (rounded down to even) |
| `threads` *(more)* | int | `0` (automatic) | 0 to 16 (soft) | Encoder threads; automatic is all of this machine's logical cores but two. Fewer threads leave more to the rest of the show (video decoding, scripts) but drop frames of busy pictures sooner; 0: automatic |
| `loop` | off \| cut \| fade \| pingpong \| cut_fade | `"off"` |  | After recording stops, also write a loop of the file as <name>_loop: a movie a player can repeat without a jump. The node shows looping... until it is written; off: no loop; cut: keeps the stretch whose end looks most like its start, at least loop_min long; for content that comes back to similar pictures; fade: cross-fades the last loop_fade seconds into the start; works for any content, the fade may show as a soft double picture; pingpong: plays forward, then backward; seamless, motion reverses at both ends; cut_fade: cuts, then cross-fades over the seam that remains |
| `loop_min` *(more)* | float | `5` | 1 to 60 s (soft) | Shortest loop `cut` may keep. A longer minimum repeats less often but may find a worse seam |
| `loop_fade` *(more)* | float | `1` | 0.1 to 10 s (soft) | Length of the cross-fade at the seam. The loop gets this much shorter than the recording |

## Component ports

The input and output sockets of a component, one pair per data kind. They sit inside a `comp.base`. Whatever is wired to the component's socket outside comes out of its `in` node inside. Whatever is wired into an `out` node inside comes out of the component's socket. Grouping nodes into a component adds the ports where wires cross its edge.

[tex.in](#texin), [tex.out](#texout), [chan.in](#chanin), [chan.out](#chanout), [audio.in](#audioin), [audio.out](#audioout), [table.in](#tablein), [table.out](#tableout), [geo.in](#geoin), [geo.out](#geoout), [mat.in](#matin), [mat.out](#matout), [light.in](#lightin), [light.out](#lightout), [view.in](#viewin), [view.out](#viewout)

### tex.in

Component input: one input socket of the component this node sits in. Whatever is wired to that socket outside comes out of this node. Cameras, files and streams come in through other nodes

Inside a component: one of its inputs.

Inputs:

- `in` (tex)

Outputs: `out` (tex).

### tex.out

Component output: one output socket of the component this node sits in. Whatever is wired into this node comes out of that socket outside. Files, projectors and streams are written by the `out` nodes

Inside a component: one of its outputs.

Inputs:

- `in` (tex)

Outputs: `out` (tex).
